answer.rationale: The binding constraints are the 18% spend cut and the 14-day expiry against a line at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer. That combination rules out any action that introduces migration or qualification work this cycle: switching primary vendor (memory_c2) and adding a second source (memory_c3) both carry onboarding lead time we cannot absorb, and defer_decision (memory_c5) is not transferable because memory_c5 explicitly concerned a non-critical service that could fall to month-to-month terms, whereas this is the primary supply contract that does not auto-renew. Straight renewal (memory_c1) protects delivery but delivers no cost movement. Negotiating at renewal is the only lever that touches cost without touching the supply path, and memory_c4 records that market-rate benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms; memory_c6 suggests a multi-year term is an additional concession axis that cut unit cost without narrowing service scope. I chose to verify memory_c2 rather than a memory supporting my intended action, because memory_c2 is the only inherited record claiming a sharp unit-cost reduction of the magnitude the 18% mandate demands, and it is the one memory that could overturn my choice. I need the original record to see whether that cut applied to a comparable primary-volume, integration-dependent component or to a smaller peripheral spend, and what the actual onboarding duration was as opposed to the summary word 'quick'. If it turns out to be genuinely comparable and onboardable inside 14 days, switching becomes live; if not, the consolidated phrasing is overstating transferability and negotiation is clearly correct. Risk I am flagging: negotiating hard under a mandated 18% target against a sole supplier we cannot walk away from creates real leverage asymmetry, and the likely concession the incumbent offers is a quieter narrowing of service scope, deprioritized allocation, or a longer lock-in that costs us optionality in the next shortage. Any negotiated price must be checked against unchanged service scope and allocation priority, not price alone, or we will book a paper saving and pay for it in delivery. I also note the inherited memory set is uniformly success-framed with no recorded failures, which is itself a reason to hold these lessons loosely; none of them state the base rates or the cases where these moves went badly, and 18% may simply not be reachable in one cycle without accepting risk finance has not priced.
